implementation_notes: The JDK already ships the combinator layer: Predicate<T> is the carrier, and()/or() combine two predicates on the same input, negate() precomposes the negation, Predicate.not(...) gives the point-free form and Predicate.isEqual(ref) is equality. contramap is a lambda over a projection (Function<T, U> plus a predicate on U), and because Java has no higher-kinded types the JDK has no monoidal verdict - accumulate failures in a List<Violation> yourself or hand the job to Bean Validation (second variant). choose is a switch pattern over a sealed interface (Java 21), which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness.
pitfalls: and()/or() return a boolean and short-circuit: no reason, no field path, no accumulation - user-facing validation needs an explicit error-collecting validator.

Predicates are generic and boxed: Predicate<Integer> and Predicate<Long> cannot be reused across numeric types, so write rules against a projection (Function<T, Integer>) rather than the raw value type.
and(other) requires the same input type, so a rule written for a domain field cannot be attached to a DTO without an adapter lambda - the adaptation is easy to duplicate and drift.

variants.name: Bean Validation constraints (declarative, accumulating)
variants.implementation_notes: Bean Validation makes the rule declarative: an annotation parameterises the check, a ConstraintValidator<A, T> implements initialize(A) and isValid(T, ConstraintValidatorContext), and @Valid on fields composes validators recursively (the closest Java gets to divide), while Validator.validate returns a set of ConstraintViolations - all failures with property paths, the accumulating verdict the pure-Predicate realization lacks. Conditional and cross-field rules need class-level constraints or groups, because a field-level validator cannot see sibling fields.
pitfalls: ConstraintValidator instances are managed and cached by the implementation and must be thread-safe: keeping state in fields across isValid calls leaks between validations.
A field-level constraint cannot see sibling fields, so cross-field invariants need a class-level constraint (@Constraint(validatedBy = ...) on the type) or a group, not a smarter field validator.
